      <content name="title">Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapy</span></span> for Menopause</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">ERT</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Estrogen Replacement <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapy</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">HRT</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hormone Replacement <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapy</span></span></content>

      <content name="altTitle">Menopausal Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapy</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> for menopause?<p>Menopause is the time in a woman's life when her menstrual periods stop.  It is a normal part of aging. During menopause, the body makes much lower amounts of the hormones estrogen and progesterone.</p><p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> for menopause involves taking estrogen, with or without progesterone (or a similar hormone called progestin). The goal is to replace some of the hormones the body no longer makes and help relieve menopausal symptoms.</p>What does hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> for menopause <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treat</span></span>?<p>In the years leading up to menopause, and during menopause, hormone levels can rise and fall. These changes can cause symptoms for some women that may be mild and go away on their own. For others, symptoms may be more severe and affect daily life.</p><p>Lower hormone levels during menopause can cause symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>Hot flashes</li><li>Night sweats</li><li>Mood changes</li><li>Vaginal dryness</li><li>Pain during sex</li></ul><p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> may help relieve these symptoms. It may also help protect against osteoporosis.</p>Who should not use hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> for menopause?<p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> is not right for everyone. You should not use hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> for menopause if you:</p><ul><li>Are pregnant or think that you may be pregnant</li><li>Have unexplained vaginal bleeding</li><li>Have had certain types of cancer</li><li>Have had a stroke or heart attack</li><li>Have had blood clots</li><li>Have liver disease</li></ul><p>Talk with your health care provider about your medical history before starting hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>.</p>What are the types of hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> for menopause?<p>There are different types of hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> for menopause. If you had surgery to remove your uterus (hysterectomy) your provider may recommend estrogen only <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>. If you still have your uterus, your provider may recommend estrogen plus progesterone (or progestin) <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>.</p><p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> for menopause comes in several forms. Most are pills taken by mouth, but there are also skin patches, gels or sprays, vaginal creams, tablets, or rings.</p><p>Your provider can help you choose the type and form that's best for you.</p>What are the risks of hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> for menopause?<p>Hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> has some risks. For some women, it may increase the risk of:</p><ul><li>Blood clots</li><li>Heart attack</li><li>Stroke</li><li>Breast cancer</li><li>Gallbladder disease</li></ul><p>The level of risk depends on the type of hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>, how long it is used, and your medical history and lifestyle.</p><p>You and your provider should talk about the risks and benefits. If you decide to use hormone <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>, it is usually recommended to use the lowest dose that helps and for the shortest time needed. Ask your provider how often you should follow up. Many recommend checking in every three to six months at first, then once a year after <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span> is working well. </p><p>Food and Drug Administration</p></content>

      <content name="title">Cancer Alternative <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapies</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Alternative <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapy</span></span> for Cancer</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are complementary and alternative <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapies</span></span> for cancer care?<p>You have many choices to make about your cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span>. One choice you might consider is using complementary and alternative medicine (CAM). CAM is the term for medical products and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapies</span></span> that are not part of standard medical care.</p><p>CAM for cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span> involves caring for your mind, body, and spirit. Some methods focus on your breathing or body movements to help you relax. Other CAM <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapies</span></span> may use special foods, supplements, or diets. Examples of CAM <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapies</span></span> include acupuncture, chiropractic, and herbal medicines.</p><p>CAM claims can sound promising, but often, researchers don't know how safe some are or how well they work. Studies are ongoing to find out the safety and usefulness of many of these methods.</p>How are complementary and alternative <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapies</span></span> used for cancer care?<p>If you're thinking about using CAM along with your standard care, it's called integrative medicine. Some methods, such as acupuncture, might help with nausea, pain, and other side effects of cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span>.</p><p>A few reasons that people with cancer may use CAM include to:</p><ul><li>Help cope with the side effects of cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatments</span></span></li><li>Ease worries about cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span> and related stress</li><li>Feel that they are doing something more to help their care</li></ul><p>CAM <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatments</span></span> don't work for everyone. Some products might interact with your other medicines. Talk to your health care provider about all the different types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span> you use. Your provider can help you make sure that everything you're using for your cancer care works well together.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/rehabilitation.html">
      <content name="title">Rehabilitation</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Occupational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapy</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Physical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapy</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rehab</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is rehabilitation?<p>Rehabilitation is care that can help you get back, keep, or improve abilities that you need for daily life. These abilities may be physical, mental, and/or cognitive (thinking and learning). You may have lost them because of a disease or injury, or as a side effect from a medical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span>. Rehabilitation can improve your daily life and functioning.</p>Who needs rehabilitation?<p>Rehabilitation is for people who have lost abilities that they need for daily life. Some of the most common causes include:</p><ul><li>Injuries and trauma, including burns, fractures (broken bones), traumatic brain injury, and spinal cord injuries</li><li>Stroke</li><li>Severe infections</li><li>Major surgery</li><li>Side effects from medical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatments</span></span>, such as from cancer <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatments</span></span></li><li>Certain birth defects and genetic disorders</li><li>Developmental disabilities</li><li>Chronic pain, including back and neck pain</li></ul>What are the goals of rehabilitation?<p>The overall goal of rehabilitation is to help you get your abilities back and regain independence. But the specific goals are different for each person. They depend on what caused the problem, whether the cause is ongoing or temporary, which abilities you lost, and how severe the problem is. For example,:</p><ul><li>A person who has had a stroke may need rehabilitation to be able to dress or bathe without help</li><li>An active person who has had a heart attack may go through cardiac rehabilitation to try to return to exercising</li><li>Someone with a lung disease may get pulmonary rehabilitation to be able to breathe better and improve their quality of life</li></ul>What happens in a rehabilitation program?<p>When you get rehabilitation, you often have a team of different health care providers helping you. They will work with you to figure out your needs, goals, and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span> plan. The types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatments that may be in a treatment</span></span> plan include:</p><ul><li>Assistive devices, which are tools, equipment, and products that help people with disabilities move and function</li><li>Cognitive rehabilitation <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> to help you relearn or improve skills such as thinking, learning, memory, planning, and decision making</li><li>Mental health counseling</li><li>Music or art <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> to help you express your feelings, improve your thinking, and develop social connections</li><li>Nutritional counseling</li><li>Occupational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> to help you with your daily activities</li><li>Physical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> to help your strength, mobility, and fitness</li><li>Recreational <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> to improve your emotional well-being through arts and crafts, games, relaxation training, and animal-assisted <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span></li><li>Speech-language <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> to help with speaking, understanding, reading, writing and swallowing</li><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Treatment</span></span> for pain</li><li>Vocational rehabilitation to help you build skills for going to school or working at a job</li></ul><p>Depending on your needs, you may have rehabilitation in the providers' offices, a hospital, or an inpatient rehabilitation center. In some cases, a provider may come to your home. If you get care in your home, you will need to have family members or friends who can come and help with your rehabilitation.</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/genesandgenetherapy.html">
      <content name="title">Genes and Gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapy</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Human Genome Project</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are genes?<p>Genes are sections of DNA in your cells that are passed down (inherited) from your parents. You inherit two copies of each gene, one from each parent. Genes carry information that controls what you look like and how your body works.</p><p>There are about 20,000 genes that provide instructions for making proteins, which your body needs to work correctly.</p><p>Some genes don't make proteins themselves but instead help control how other genes work. They act like switches, turning other genes on or off. This means they help decide when, where, and how much of a protein is made in your body.</p>What happens when genes change?<p>Changes in your genes are also called gene variants or mutations. These changes can be inherited, occur as you age, or result from environmental factors such as chemicals or radiation. Often, these changes have no effect, but sometimes, even a small change in the DNA can alter the instructions for making proteins. If genes don't make the right proteins, or don't make them correctly, this can cause a genetic disorder.</p>What is gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>?<p>Gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> uses genes to <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treat</span></span> or prevent disease by correcting genetic problems. It works by changing your genetic material, rather than relying on traditional <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatments</span></span> like medicine or surgery.</p><p>New genetic material can be delivered into cells in two main ways:</p><ul><li>ex-vivo <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span>. Cells are removed from your body, modified by adding genetic material, and then placed back into your body.</li><li>in-vivo <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span>. Genetic material is delivered directly into your body, often through an injection.</li></ul><p>A common form of gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> involves inserting a normal gene to replace an abnormal gene. Other approaches include:</p><ul><li>Repairing an abnormal gene</li><li>Altering the degree to which a gene is turned on or off</li></ul><p>Newer techniques offer different ways to correct genetic problems:</p><ul><li>Genome editing (also called gene editing). Instead of adding new genetic material into cells, this approach changes the DNA that's already in your cells. A well-known example is CRISPR-Cas9. This promising technique is still being studied and may soon be used to <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treat</span></span> genetic disorders.</li><li>Cell-based gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> combines gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> and cell <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>. An example of this would be CAR T cell <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>. Cells, which are often immune system cells, are genetically altered to help <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treat</span></span> a disease and then introduced into the body.</li></ul><p>Gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapies</span></span> are currently only approved to <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treat</span></span> a small number of diseases, such as:</p><ul><li>Leber congenital amaurosis, an inherited eye disorder.</li><li>Spinal muscular atrophy, a genetic muscle disorder.</li></ul>What are the risks and challenges of gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>?<p>While gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> holds great promise, it comes with risks and challenges. Studies are still ongoing to ensure these <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatments</span></span> are safe and effective. Some challenges include:</p><ul><li>Immune system reactions. Your body may see the new material as a threat and react to it.</li><li>Unintended effects. Changes to DNA could affect other genes in harmful ways.</li><li>High costs. Gene <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapies</span></span> are often expensive and are not widely accessible.</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/oxygentherapy.html">
      <content name="title">Oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Therapy</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hyperbaric Oxygen</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is oxygen?<p>Oxygen is a gas that your body needs to work properly. Your cells need oxygen to make energy. Your lungs absorb oxygen from the air you breathe. The oxygen enters your blood from your lungs and travels to your organs and body tissues.</p><p>Certain medical conditions can cause your blood oxygen levels to be too low. Low blood oxygen may make you feel short of breath, tired, and confused. It can also damage your body. Oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> can help you get more oxygen.</p>What is oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>?<p>Oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy is a treatment</span></span> that provides you with extra oxygen to breathe in. It is also called supplemental oxygen. It is only available through a prescription from your health care provider. You may get it in the hospital, another medical setting, or at home. Some people only need it for a short period of time. Others will need long-term oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>.</p><p>There are different types of devices that can give you oxygen. Some use tanks of liquid or gas oxygen. Others use an oxygen concentrator, which pulls oxygen out of the air. You will get the oxygen through a nose tube (cannula), a mask, or a tent. The extra oxygen is breathed in along with normal air.</p><p>There are portable versions of the tanks and oxygen concentrators. They can make it easier for you to move around while using your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>.</p>Who needs oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>?<p>You may need oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> if you have a condition that causes low blood oxygen, such as:</p><ul><li>COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)</li><li>Pneumonia</li><li>COVID-19</li><li>A severe asthma attack</li><li>Late-stage heart failure</li><li>Cystic fibrosis</li><li>Sleep apnea</li></ul>What are the risks of using oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>?<p>Oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> is generally safe, but it can cause side effects. They include a dry or bloody nose, tiredness, and morning headaches.</p><p>Oxygen poses a fire risk, so you should never smoke or use flammable materials when using oxygen. If you use oxygen tanks, make sure your tank is secured and stays upright. If it falls and cracks or the top breaks off, the tank can fly like a missile.</p>What is hyperbaric oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>?<p>Hyperbaric oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span> (HBOT) is a different type of oxygen <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">therapy</span></span>. It involves breathing oxygen in a pressurized chamber or tube. That allows your lungs to gather up to three times more oxygen than you would get by breathing oxygen at normal air pressure. The extra oxygen moves through your blood and to your organs and body tissues.</p><p>HBOT is used to <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treat</span></span> certain serious wounds, burns, injuries, and infections. It also <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treats</span></span> air or gas embolisms (bubbles of air in your bloodstream), decompression sickness suffered by divers, and carbon monoxide poisoning.</p><p>But some <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treatment</span></span> centers claim that HBOT can <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">treat</span></span> almost anything, including Alzheimer's disease, autism, cancer, and Lyme disease. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not cleared or approved the use of HBOT for these conditions. There are risks to using HBOT, so always check with your provider before you try it.</p></content>
